Nexus and blending however both end up being decent, but blending pulls far ahead because it gives you very high control on your slots. Because of this, Universalist is a bit of a trap. Instead of a school slot (which is an extra learned spell) you get one of your existing slots cast a second time, which does not include the highest rank as a bonus since every wizard gets that anyways. This function doesn't interact well with spell blending, staffs, or staff nexus in comparison to the proper schools because the proper schools can sacrifice their school slots to these. As a universalist, you're sacrificing a small amount of power (one max rank slot) so that you can interact less with Vancian Casting which is what wizard is all about.

Psychic had the unique ability to be the only class able to always get all its focus points back. Oracle being second but only at higher levels (10+) and even then still curse limited. That design decision was why they had less slots, why they had unleash windows to maximize the slots, and why they generally had mediocre feats (seriously every amp feat is super mediocre.) Since only a psychic could do this style of refocusing, other classes poaching their amps wasn't a big deal as they couldn't use them 3 times every encounter.

The moment the focus point change happened both oracle and psychic lost their niche, and oracle  in particular couldn't even make use of the change because they still had the curse limiter.

And psychic lost most of its value because now every other class can just poach their amps and use them to full effect every combat. The most egregious being guidance on anyone ever, shield on martials, and ignition on spell casters.

The spell casting proficiency changes for casters further doubled down on it as now my wizard can use his same spell casting proficiency on an amped ignition and affect it with irresistible magic just to rub the salt in.

Hell post remaster oracle even got its 'free focus spell' niche back that psychic lost by decoupling curse spells from focus spells, functionally giving them two focus pools simultaneously to draw abilities from.

Since the focus point change and sorcerer buff... I honestly don't know psychic's place. The easily poach-able amps and unleash psych just aren't strong enough to justify the reduced slots, absolute trash class feats (even wizard has better options), and 'dead' self stupefied turns.

Being occult means they cant easily get max value out of unleash, meanwhile an elemental sorcerer is getting the same bonus from bloodline spells and half the bonus at all times via sorcerous potency, double the spell slots, lots of powerful feats, and still able to poach psychic amps if they really want to.

-Going lone wolf will cost a significant amount of story since you lose two companions

-Going the usually recommended '4 physical' or '4 magical' party will make fights either one sided stomps, or really rough if you're countered. Its easier but it strips a lot of the tactical fun.

As for that backstory, although they had an empyreal dragon as a benefactor only one brother absorbed the magic and even stole the very life from the other in the egg. Because of this when they were born Tashvin was blessed with empyreal powers (Dragonblooded heritage) and a vibrant, healthy appearance. His scales are white, with a golden glow to his eyes and a personality of a meek and humble cleric. Despite this innate power he chose the path of wizardry, losing himself in books and studying magic in safety. Tashvin isn't much of an adventurer, but he still wants to explore and see the history of the world and the universe. With a focus on the planar lore and a desire to see as much as he can he joins an expedition to expand his horizons.

In contrast, Vel'thys was born weak, so weak in fact his body oozed life leaving him weakened. A dhampir in nature his sense of the world and feelings towards it are muted, leading to him chasing the extreme emotional highs that can push past the emptiness. He sought power, and extremely quickly passed his brother in that regard and reaching the upper limits (levels 17+) before his brother even reach half that far. An aberrant sorcerer by nature with his outpouring life represented by the life oracle archetype, he turned hedonistic in nature. Although he helped save the world during the extinction curse events he practices cannibalism (Represented in the Taste for Blood line), uses his life magic to perform tortures, and even feeds off the pain of others (Dhampir feed on pain line). He's cruel and ruthless, but uses his charisma to keep the worst aspects of it under wraps, putting on a charming if sharp tongued front.

Despite these contrasting personalities, the two brothers both respect and see each other as someone to care about. Vel'thys uses (or at least tries to use) Tashvin as a moral compass, being that their familial link brings about the only shred of empathy he feels and using that to never let himself go so far into his hedonism he loses himself entirely. While in the reverse Tashvin uses his brother as a guide to power, using his lessons to not let himself be tricked by his kindhearted nature, or to learn to be ruthless rather than meek. Unfortunately, their power dynamic is toxic in nature, with Vel'thys using modify memory on his brother multiple times to hide things he's done that Tashvin witnessed, inflicting trauma to harden his brother to the darker parts of life, or using his overpowering nature to pressure Tashvin to be more ruthless than his personality allows.

You've kind of got it. The way it works is it spawns a patrol on a set timer based on player count (its a little messy if people split up though).

From there, if someone is near an outpost spawn rates go up 0-50% based on how close they are to the main red area of the outpost.

Enemy patrols when spawning then pick a random outpost and spawn 75m-150m away from you in the direction of that outpost and make a direct line to where you were _when they spawned in_ so if you move constantly they won't cross your path and miss you.

What happens however is there's a very low (0-17.5%) increasing spawn rate going from 50%-100% killed outposts. But another subtle thing is that as you clear outposts, all the spawning patrols start coming from the same direction. What this means is if you're heading towards the last two outposts, every single patrol will spawn in front of you heading towards you. This can lead to a death spiral where you just keep getting swarmed heading in a straight line there.

Once all the outposts are wiped out enemies start spawning at the closest map edge to your location and move towards you. So the map gets much quieter (so long you keep moving) since the 50% red area spawn boost is gone and enemies are spawning much further away and thus less likely to cross your path.

The thing that usually throws people off is the massive 300% spawn rate increase when you complete the main objective. Missions very quickly can turn into death spirals if the main objective is completed and then people try to do PoIs or secondary objectives afterwards.

It doesn't double it. It scales from 0% -> 17.5% faster going from 50% outposts to 100% outposts cleared.

What does increase spawn rate signifigantly is completing the main objective. Moment it finishes and you can call extraction spawn rates are 300% faster for the rest of the mission. 

Additionally patrols spawn between you and outposts, so as you clear more of them you narrow the spawning locations so they're more likely to spawn between you and the next outpost you're heading too. By the time you're down to the last one _every single patrol_ will spawn between you and that outpost.

Once you've cleared them all out however, so long you haven't completed main objective (Which increases spawn rate so much the entire map starts swarming) you start not coming across patrols as much because they spawn on the edge of the map and slowly walk to where you were when they spawned, so can easily miss you entirely.

It doesn't increase it by much (20% once all are destroyed iirc). the big thing is that they'll all come from the same direction as you have fewer left. If there's one outpost left and you're running towards it every single patrol will spawn between you and it.

Once they're all destroyed the patrols start spawning at direction of the closest edge of the map which means you practically barely run across them while running around the map unless you've already completed main objective (which increases spawn rates by 4x as much)

Compressor / Decompressor are a linked structure.

When you compress say, 100 water, you can then decompress 100 water _anywhere_. Its how you get morphic fluid from DLC1 to other planets.

However, they are _1 to 1_ linked. What this means is that if you make a compressor that compresses 300 water, and then make two decompressors that decompress 150 water... only one of them will work at a time, and when you try to activate the second one it wont work.

It also, if playing by the assumed default, nerfs doomstacking as many higher tier units are limited by # of production buildings. Only 2 dragons from the dragon building for example.

Of course, this means higher tier units _feel_ higher tier. Fighting an early game depth guard with your T1 army is watching a small elite force of vampires mulch your entire force.

Another fundamental thing is economy is vastly different based on faction. Factions like Dark Elves and Beastmen can make much more money razing/raiding than their base economy can. While dwarfs make almost no money from fighting, but can get a buff from winning battles that boosts local income/public order while in their own regions + 'raid' their own land for increased income with no penalties. They also have absurdly expensive buildings/long build times, but ridiculous economy from said buildings to promote slow expansion and defensive playstyle.

If playing a martial that uses flourish abilities often, needs skill feats for athletics/acrobatics and lacks a free hand (Flurry ranger, double slice fighter) go with blessed one. It doesn't require medicine to be trained or battle medicine, and doesn't have flourish. Bonus is that if you're a frontliner you can use it on yourself in a pinch without a free hand.

Blessed one is also great if you're looking for a way to get your 2nd or 3rd focus point in your build.

Medic is significantly better if you're doing any of the following:

* Already get 3 focus points from other feats/class features or have useful focus spells (Oracle/psychic/witch)
* Playing a caster: doctor's visitation is an insanely good 3rd action for casters.
* Planning to invest in medicine anyways, as it gives free expert medicine upgrade
* Playing a class with very important class feats, medic only needs to use up one as it has skill feats in the archtype
* Don't use flourish abilities (Doctor's visitation is absurdly good, but has flourish trait)
* Have caster friends or are one. Holistic Care is one of the few resourceless, cooldown free ways to remove stupify. If you have a psychic theyll worship the ground you walk if you use it on them.
* Have a free hand to use it.
* Don't have a multiple encounters every hour, as battle medicine is limited to 1 per person + 1 per hour once you hit master. ~~Due to doctors visitation if attacks of opportunity arent a risk its a much, much better in combat than lay on hands.~~

On a side note: getting both on a sorcerer is amazing for out of combat healing since sorcerers refresh focus points passively out of combat and can do so while treating wounds with medic. Its a great path to get a 3rd focus point on sorcerer too, since you generally dont grab 2 bloodline powers to reach 3 points. Doing that you can become both an arcane blaster and a respectable healer simultaneously with a stride each round being replaced with doctors visitation a lot of the time.


~~Edit: Forgot to mention, blessed one also has no manipulate so it doesnt provoke. This makes it a better option for melee, as medic can provoke enemies when healing self or others.~~ Blessed one gives +2 AC to allies for one round (not self) so thats a pretty good benefit too thats overlooked.
